title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
hook: a clay Ganesha carried home under a cloth, drums in the street, and a moon nobody is supposed to look at
carry: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: a fast, a cradle, and midnight. What did you wait for, and did you wait well? Today, a god who arrives at your front door, made of clay. Day one hundred forty-six.

In Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see a family walking home from the market carrying a Ganesha about the size of a toddler. His face is covered with a cloth. A cousin is banging a drum. The kids are shouting Ganpati Bappa Morya. He's made of clay, still slightly damp. At home, a corner has been cleared, a little platform set up, flowers ready. They'll uncover his face only once he's in his seat. For the next few days he's a guest, fed, sung to, visited. Then they'll carry him back out and give him to the water. Today, the arrival.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, FACE COVERED.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA.` → `A GUEST FOR A FEW DAYS.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth day, the fourth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, and that's the day Ganesha is said to have been born. And why clay? Go back to the very first story on this path. Parvati makes a son from earth, from the paste of her own bath, and sets him to guard her door. Ganesha begins as something shaped by hand. So the clay makes sense: once a year, families shape him again, or bring home one that's been shaped. At home the image is set on its seat, and a priest or an elder performs prana pratishtha, inviting life into it. From that moment he's treated as present. He gets fresh flowers, blades of durva grass, which he's said to love, and modak, the sweet dumplings he's always holding. Arti morning and evening. Here's a surprise from history. For a long time this was mostly a festival inside homes. Then in 1893, in Pune, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public festival, with Ganeshas in the street, where whole neighborhoods could gather, under British rule, with a god everyone loved. Today some public Ganeshas are two stories tall. And one odd custom. On this night, many people won't look at the moon. The story people tell: the moon laughed at Ganesha, round and full of sweets, after a tumble, and Ganesha cursed him, so anyone who looks at the moon that night will be falsely accused. It's a funny story with a sharp point: mocking someone costs you more than it costs them.
screen: `CHATURTHI, THE FOURTH DAY.` · `HE BEGAN AS EARTH SHAPED BY HAND.` · `INVITED IN, AND TREATED AS PRESENT.` · `1893: THE FESTIVAL GOES PUBLIC.` · then, large: `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a guest. Settle, and breathe. Picture your front door. Someone is carrying Ganesha in, face covered, drums behind him. Where would you seat him? Clear that spot in your mind: the pile of mail, the laptop, the shoes. Put down a small cloth. Set him there. Now lift the cloth from his face. What would you offer first: a flower, a sweet, a few blades of grass? Stay with him a while, the way you'd sit with a guest who's just arrived and has nowhere to be. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. The fourth day, Ganesha's birthday, when he's brought home in clay and treated as a guest.
Your line: Ganesh Chaturthi, the clay idol, the immersion. Today, clear one small space, a shelf, a corner of a desk, as if a guest were coming. Day one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: On Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindus bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, invite his presence with prana pratishtha, and honor him daily with flowers, durva grass, modak and arti for one and a half to ten days.

original.note: Sanskrit: Ganesha, lord of the ganas, and chaturthi, the fourth day of the lunar fortnight.

trapdoor: what it means: his birthday, kept by bringing him home in clay, inviting him in, and treating him as a guest.
what a scholar hears: a festival kept mostly in homes became a public one in Pune in 1893, when Tilak helped bring Ganesha into the street.

notes: Date: Shukla Chaturthi of Bhadrapada, August–September. Confirm.
Tilak's public Ganeshotsav in 1893 in Pune: standard history; some sources note earlier public celebrations (e.g. Bhausaheb Rangari). Confirm the phrasing 'helped turn it into'.

The moon story: versions differ (the moon laughs as Ganesha falls from his mouse after eating many modaks); the belief that seeing the moon brings false accusation is linked to Krishna and the Syamantaka jewel. Confirm framing as 'the story people tell'.
Prana pratishtha performed by a priest or elder at home: practice varies. Confirm.
Maharashtra as the setting of the hook (Mumbai trips the British-spelling check on "mum"), and Marathi chant 'Ganpati Bappa Morya'. Confirm.
